correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern opening and northwestward La Inmaculada approach
correspondence.finding: The Relieve original depicts the chosen opening in the drainage west of Sierra Jojobal. Its northwestward course is labeled La Inmaculada and meets the larger San Ignacio drainage at the northern turn. Nearby eastern feeders remain distinct; their presence does not give the chosen opening a surveyed source or precise name-start vertex.
correspondence.name_scope: La Inmaculada upper reach, connected to the named San Ignacio corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwestward San Ignacio reach and upper alluvial entry
correspondence.finding: The original map directly labels San Ignacio on the southwestward channel below the La Inmaculada join and depicts its continuation south into the plain east of Sierra Los Mochos. The bounded imagery overlaps the lower end of this approach and shows its branching alluvial setting. The named western branches and incoming side drainages are read as connections at regional scale, not exact confluence coordinates.
correspondence.name_scope: San Ignacio supported on this mapped reach.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected southward alluvial continuation and approach to Aribaipa
correspondence.finding: The municipal original sends the labeled San Ignacio drainage southwest toward the La Tinaja junction, while the selected continuation runs farther south through the interposed alluvial tract toward Aribaipa. The independent imagery shows diffuse branching washes, pale and vegetated swales, and narrow straight or angular modified features across this tract. The southern broad channel and its incoming washes are visible, but a continuous selected upper-to-southern through-corridor cannot be confidently distinguished from the neighboring branches and modified lines. The open issue is a meaningful branch transfer across the plain, not a demand for identical banks, every minor bend, or flowing water on the image date.
correspondence.name_scope: No whole-system or local reach name assigned to the unresolved alluvial link.

correspondence.component_scope: Aribaipa receiving corridor and northwestward passage through the low ridge
correspondence.finding: The southern imagery detail depicts the broad east–west channel and its westward narrowing. On the municipal original the selected westward then northwestward course follows the channel at the Aribaipa junction, through the low ridge east of Cerro El Puerto, toward the western receiving drainage. This lower corridor is independently visible even though its selected connection from the north remains unresolved.
correspondence.name_scope: Aribaipa identifies an incoming eastern drainage; it is not extended as a scalar over the selected mainstem.

correspondence.component_scope: Western convergences near La Tinaja and Los Arenales
correspondence.finding: The Relieve original depicts the lower northwestward approach joining the western channel system below the La Tinaja/San Ignacio approaches, then running west past the Los Arenales convergence and bending south beside Cerro El Puerto. These are mapped connected channels, with no required intervening lake or reservoir crossing.
correspondence.name_scope: Lower receiving drainage of the San Ignacio coastal system; individual branch names remain bounded to their map labels.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual final coastal passage and Gulf terminal
correspondence.finding: The final selected part follows the mapped southward coastal channel west of Cerro El Puerto and then its southwestward opening to the Gulf of California. The locality map places this outlet in the coastal setting north of Desemboque de Los Seris. The selected endpoint is the Gulf coast, not an inland Aribaipa junction or a terminal lake. No current mouth opening, tidal channel allocation or precise shoreline position is asserted.
correspondence.name_scope: Gulf of California receiving water; no scalar river name assigned to the sea.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected initial opening, westward inland route and first northward continuation
correspondence.finding: The model opening, westward traverse and turn north can be oriented, but the readable sources do not independently locate the opening or continuously establish this upper fragment. The report’s general directional account is insufficient to assign its name to each part.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward middle/lower-river candidate; not a completed label for every selected part
correspondence.finding: The selected course proceeds north toward the El Charco setting. Authorial locality evidence supports the candidate, while substantial upstream through-links and both fragment connections remain untraced on permitted primary geography.

The named receiving-river and coastal setting are supported. The specific selected estuarine continuation and final passage have not been independently matched; regional mouth identity alone is not full correspondence.

The selected opening is the northwestern end of the north-to-south corridor. The original regional maps distinguish the upper Zaza drainage from Hacha and Caonao tributary subbasins, but do not securely identify the actual selected opening and its first southeastward connection. No surveyed natural source or headwater hydronym is assigned.

The authored maps and topology identify a Zaza receiving system with distinct incoming Hacha, Caonao, Calabazas, Tuinucú, Yayabo and Taguasco drainage. The selected long southeastward and then southward course is consistent at broad regional scale with the Zaza side of this two-basin study. Basin inclusion and the river label on an abstract topology do not by themselves establish every selected intermediate join.
correspondence.component_name_role: Regional receiving-river candidate, not an established name for the complete selected interval.

correspondence.finding: Slide9 explicitly names Embalse Zaza and separately depicts the smaller Tuinucú and Siguaney impoundments. Slide12 carries their distinct branches into the Zaza reservoir node. This supports the large regional impoundment setting of the selected lower-middle corridor, without establishing that every selected approach and reservoir-exit leg follows the corresponding mapped channel. Reservoir surfaces retain their own identity.
correspondence.component_name_role: Named regional impoundment context; exact selected inlet-to-outlet correspondence remains partial.

correspondence.finding: The study distinguishes the river below the Zaza reservoir from Canal Magistral, a small-hydropower component and the agricultural supply network toward Sur del Jíbaro. The eastern Jatibonico del Sur system includes Lebrije, Dignoráh and La Felicidad as separately depicted reservoirs. These are not river aliases or proof that the selected line uses a diversion. The final southern selection makes an extended westward turn before its coastal ending; the small geographic maps and non-geographic topology do not establish the full natural-channel or managed-link correspondence of that turn.
correspondence.component_name_role: Lower receiving-system context, not a confirmed name for every selected southern leg.

correspondence.finding: Slide6 names Mar Caribe and geographically separates the Zaza coastal drainage from the eastern Jatibonico del Sur outlet. The selected tip lies in the western coastal receiving setting rather than at the eastern Jatibonico outlet. The regional map does not independently establish which final channel, estuarine wetland connection or specific mouth carries the actual selected westward-then-southward end. No lagoon, lake, wetland or mouth name is invented.

The chosen southern opening corresponds to a narrow, snow-patterned upland valley. Its corridor proceeds north, bends northeast and continues into the more open downstream valley. Patchy snow obscures small channel details, but the valley and ordinary route correspondence are readable; no exact bank or current-flow claim is required.

The selected short northward pieces continue along the same incised-to-open river valley. Visible channel bends and lateral drainage arrivals lead into the elongate-waterbody corridor to the north. Adjacent western drainage and ponds are not substituted as the main route.

The northward route passes through a series of elongated waterbodies and their narrow river connections. Several waterbodies are partly covered by snow or lake ice in the southern detail, while the overview shows their dark open-water outlines. The sequence, connecting valley and successive openings are readable at ordinary corridor scale. No individual lake name is established.

The lake-country route continues north through narrow reaches and broader waterbody margins, then becomes a more open meandering channel. Side channels and small lakes lie beside the selected corridor; the northward continuation to the eastern turn is visible.

The river turns east across a broad lowland with substantial meanders and lateral tributary arrivals. The selected stage-three line generalizes these bends, while imagery shows the continuous river corridor and its approach to the northeast-trending lower valley. Nearby ponds are contextual waterbodies, not separately named mainstem components.

At the eastern lowland bend, the continuous river enters a northeast-trending valley among ridges and elongated lakes. The coarse selected bend is south of some visible meanders, but it corresponds to this same joining valley at ordinary corridor scale. Exact channel-bank coincidence is not imposed, and a separate through-lake route across neighbouring lakes is not asserted.

The lower river follows the northeast-trending valley toward the coast. Narrow and locally broader reaches, side-stream joins and the approach to the low coastal outlet are visible. Large elongated lakes southeast of the river remain lateral landscape features rather than substituted portions of the selected river.

The visible river reaches the head of the western arm of Glenelg Bay through the low alluvial outlet area. The coastal arm is continuous northeastward with the receiving bay. ARC403 independently describes a delta at the head of this west arm and identifies Glenelg Bay as the southwestern extension of Wynniatt Bay. The final seaward model extension is over the receiving inlet and is not named as a natural river reach.
